## EMERGENCY 2.0

## Silencing Voices. Manufacturing Fear.

## Introduction: Andhra Pradesh's Digital Emergency

Andhra Pradesh is passing through a Digital Emergency in which
questioning the government is increasingly treated as a criminal act.
Under the Chandrababu Naidu-led coalition, political criticism is being
answered not with facts, explanations or democratic debate, but with
police notices, multiple FIRs, midnight arrests, interstate operations,
custodial intimidation, serious non-bailable charges and digital takedowns.

The crackdown began with YSRCP social media activists. It then
expanded to party spokespersons, students, women, journalists, political
analysts, YouTubers, comedians, page administrators and ordinary
citizens who raised questions concerning public expenditure, corruption or
administrative failure. The target is no longer one category of political
worker. The target is dissent itself.

What is unfolding is not a series of isolated police excesses. The same
pattern appears across districts and cases. A politically inconvenient post
is identified. A ruling-party functionary or sympathiser files a complaint.
Police register an FIR, often under provisions disproportionate to the
alleged expression. The speaker is summoned, picked up or arrested.
Phones are seized, families are denied information and arrest records are
prepared after custody has begun. The same content may produce
several FIRs in different jurisdictions. If ordinary provisions do not secure
remand, organised-crime, narcotics, extortion, sexual-offence or
extraordinary legal provisions are added.

The prosecution then serves two purposes. It punishes the person who
raised the question and supplies the official basis for asking X, Facebook,
Instagram or YouTube to restrict the content. The speaker is criminalised
while the speech disappears. By the time a court intervenes, the arrest,
humiliation, financial damage and political warning have already achieved
their purpose.

This is **Emergency 2.0**, an Emergency redesigned for the digital age.
There is no formal proclamation suspending constitutional rights. Instead,
repression is decentralised through police stations, political complainants,
special units, criminal provisions, platform notices and coordinated
propaganda. One activist receives a notice in Kadapa. Another is arrested
at midnight in West Godavari. A journalist is brought from Hyderabad. A
comedian is pursued across State boundaries. A critical video becomes
inaccessible. An official opposition page is restricted in India. Each action
appears separate; together they manufacture fear.

The earlier Emergency openly censored newspapers and imprisoned
political opponents. Emergency 2.0 uses the FIR, the seized phone, the
unmarked vehicle, the remand report, the platform request and the fear
that the next knock may come at midnight.

## 1. The Scale of the Crackdown

More than 1200 named individuals, pages, political handles and
account administrators connected with 3000 reported cases
documented through available police information, court proceedings,
media reports, victim accounts and party records. Field reports indicate
that the actual number of political cases, informal station-level summons,
threats, interrogations and unreported instances of harassment exceeds
more than that.

The documented figures reveal two parallel strategies. The first is mass
intimidation: hundreds of people face one case, notice or summons so
that fear spreads across the wider digital community. The second is
concentrated persecution: selected activists are buried under repeated
FIRs until their lives revolve around police stations, court appearances,
anticipatory bail and legal expenditure.

Of the 3000 cases, many faced two or more cases. The highest counts
show the scale of legal siege:

- Varra Ravindra Reddy — 26 cases
- Kowlepalli Amjad Khan — 24
- Dodda Rakesh Gandhi — 20
- Bhargav — 20
- Inturi Ravikiran — 19
- Munagala Harishwar Reddy — 19

The number of FIRs is itself used to create the impression that the person

government first multiplies the cases and then cites the multiplied number

must engage lawyers in different districts, arrange sureties, travel
hundreds of kilometres and remain prepared for another arrest even after

evidence was weak, the punishment has already been inflicted.

The crackdown also evolved in intensity. The first phase relied on notices,
station summons and multiple FIRs. It progressed to midnight arrests and
plainclothes pickups. It later expanded into illegal detention, custodial
abuse, targeting of families and serious non-bailable charges. The newest
phase combines interstate policing, UAPA-type escalation, platform
censorship, restriction of political pages and the creation of permanent
social-media monitoring structures.

critics are watched for content capable of embarrassing the government

The posts attracting action concern governance and public interest:
Amaravati expenditure and land acquisition, floods, fertilizer shortages,
electricity tariffs, government debt, medical-college privatisation, DSC
irregularities, TTD tenders, the Tirumala Laddu controversy, liquor and

The decisive factor is rarely whether the expression presents an

government’s narrative, attracts significant reach or questions a powerful

A few visible voices are then selected and punished publicly so that
thousands of others begin censoring themselves.

## 2.2 Manufacturing the Complaint

The government avoids directly admitting political retaliation. A
ruling-party functionary, local leader, sympathiser or politically connected
person files the complaint. Police then claim that they are merely
responding to a citizen.

In several cases, the complainant has no direct personal injury but claims
that criticism of a leader created hostility, disturbed harmony or caused
public disorder. A partisan objection is thereby dressed as a criminal
grievance.

This structure creates a false appearance of neutrality while allowing
political leaders to activate police action through party workers.

## 2.3 One Post, Multiple FIRs

The same post, video, meme or political allegation is used to generate
complaints in different districts. Each FIR requires separate legal
representation, bail and court appearances.

Relief in one case does not provide real protection because another
jurisdiction can seek custody. If bail is granted in one matter, a fresh case
can prevent release. Geography becomes an instrument of punishment.

The objective is not adjudication of one disputed statement. It is legal

## 2.4 Mass Notices and WhatsApp Intimidation

Hundreds of notices were issued during the early phase, including to
WhatsApp group administrators and members who had merely forwarded
material. People were called to stations, photographed, questioned about
account access and asked to identify creators and administrators.

Some were pressured to sign undertakings that they would not circulate
“anti-government” material.

The notice appears less severe than arrest, but when used at scale it
becomes an efficient form of censorship. One station summons frightens
an entire WhatsApp group. Administrators delete political content.
Members leave groups. Citizens stop forwarding even factual reports.

## 2.5 Reopening Years-Old Speech

Old interviews, political remarks, comedy performances and YouTube
responses are stored and revived when prosecution becomes politically
convenient.

Yagnesh faced midnight arrest over an old YouTube response. Posani
Krishna Murali’s earlier political remarks were reopened after the change
of government. Nagarjuna Yadav was arrested over statements made
nearly two years earlier.

The absence of immediate disorder when the words were originally
spoken exposes the political nature of the later action. Old speech is
treated as a permanent weapon available to the government.

The message is that no statement is ever closed. It can become
tomorrow’s FIR.

## 2.6 Midnight Arrests and Plainclothes Pickups

Where notice procedure would ordinarily be sufficient, police arrive at
night, in civil dress or in unmarked vehicles. The method creates
maximum panic and minimum transparency.

Distance offers no protection. A critic can be pursued wherever he or she
lives, works or performs.

## 2.9 Unrecorded Custody and Altered Arrest Timelines

Several cases reveal gaps between the actual pickup and the formally
recorded arrest. This unrecorded period creates a zone without
accountability.

The detainee may have no lawyer. The family may receive no information.
Phones may be searched. Statements and confessions may be prepared.
The arrest location and timing may be reconstructed later to suit the
prosecution.

Savindra Reddy’s case contained conflicting arrest timings across police
records. Varra Ravindra Reddy’s arrest was recorded after a disputed
period of detention. Krishnaveni was transported from Hyderabad before
formal arrest documentation. Tarak’s family struggled to establish his
whereabouts after he was taken.

These are not clerical mistakes. Arrest timing determines whether
constitutional safeguards were followed and whether the person was
produced within the required period.

## 2.10 Forced Signatures and Retroactive Evidence

Victims have described being made to sign blank sheets, typed papers or
statements they were not permitted to read. Once completed, these
documents enter the remand record as though they were voluntary or
contemporaneous.

Krishnaveni’s case is a prominent example. She was brought under police
control first; documentation followed. Tarak also reported coercion relating
to statements used to support serious allegations.

The sequence is reversed: detention does not follow evidence; paperwork
is created after detention to justify what has already happened.

text:
Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita became a principal weapon.
The provision is intended for organised criminal syndicates and continuing
unlawful activity. It was applied to political social media activity.

Content creators, page administrators and party workers were grouped
together and portrayed as participants in organised crime. The existence
of political coordination was presented as proof of a criminal enterprise.

Tarak Pratap Reddy and Sai Bhargav Reddy were booked under Section
111 in cases arising from social media content. Courts questioned how
cellphone posts or political communication could satisfy the elements of
organised crime.

The purpose was clear: secure remand, oppose bail, seize devices and
portray an opposition digital network as a criminal syndicate.

## 2.12 Escalation to Narcotics, Sexual-Offence and Extortion Charges

When ordinary social-media provisions fail to guarantee detention, more
stigmatizing offences are introduced.

Savindra Reddy was branded a ganja offender. Tarak faced extortion and
sexual-harassment allegations in addition to organised-crime provisions.

Such charges make bail more difficult and destroy social reputation. A
person known for questioning floods, fertilizer shortages or corruption is
suddenly described as a drug dealer or sexual offender. The accusation
dominates public discussion; the original governance question
disappears.

This is reputational execution before trial.

## 2.13 UAPA, Preventive Detention and Extraordinary Provisions

The escalation has moved towards laws normally reserved for the gravest
threats. In the Ravan case, provisions associated with terrorism were
invoked despite the controversy arising from online political expression.

Earlier proposals also sought to expand preventive-detention mechanisms
to cyber offences. This would allow social media users to be detained
without the safeguards of an ordinary criminal trial.

The progression is visible:

## 2.14 Custodial Violence, Caste Abuse and Humiliation

Custody itself becomes punishment. Sai Bhargav reported that he was beaten, leading the court to record his statement in camera and order medical examination.

Puli Sagar, a Dalit youth who questioned a ruling-party MLA’s claims, was
stripped, assaulted, abused with caste slurs and threatened inside a
police station.

The purpose is larger than extracting information. Public knowledge that
one critic was beaten or humiliated is intended to silence an entire political
or social community.

## 2.15 Targeting Families and Livelihoods

The case may formally name one person, but the punishment is imposed
on the entire household.

Sudharani’s husband was detained separately while travelling with their
children, leaving the children stranded and traumatised. Savindra’s wife
was forced to search for him and approach the High Court. Tarak’s elderly
parents moved between stations seeking information.

Vehicles, businesses, employment and income are also vulnerable. Some
activists lose access to phones required for work. Others spend their
earnings on lawyers and travel. Daily-wage workers lose income for every
police or court appearance.

The government expects families to pressure activists into silence.

## 2.16 Media Parade and Criminal Branding

Before judicial scrutiny, the accused may be photographed between
officers, presented with a covered face or described through the harshest
section in the FIR.

## 2.17 Bail Suppression and Jail-to-Jail Transfers

The playbook continues after remand. Police oppose bail, delay
documentation, activate fresh cases and move accused persons between
jurisdictions.

Posani Krishna Murali’s multiple cases enabled jail-to-jail transfers. Relief
in one matter did not guarantee release because another police unit could
seek production.

The process becomes a revolving door:

Arrest → remand → bail → fresh arrest → new remand.

The government does not need conviction to keep a critic trapped in
custody and litigation.

## 2.18 Silencing the Speech After Silencing the Speaker

The FIR is then used to approach digital platforms. Police ask X,
Facebook, Instagram or YouTube to remove or geographically restrict the
underlying content.

The complaint therefore punishes both the speaker and the speech.

The user may receive no meaningful opportunity to respond before
restriction. The police agency investigating the case effectively becomes
the body initiating censorship of the disputed material.

## 2.19 Selective Protection for Ruling-Party Content

The same urgency is absent when ruling-party networks circulate
morphed images, degrading attacks, content targeting women or abusive

documentation, activate fresh cases and move accused persons between
jurisdictions.

in one matter did not guarantee release because another police unit could
seek production.

The process becomes a revolving door:

Arrest → remand → bail → fresh arrest → new remand.

The government does not need conviction to keep a critic trapped in
custody and litigation.

underlying content.

The complaint therefore punishes both the speaker and the speech.

The user may receive no meaningful opportunity to respond before
restriction. The police agency investigating the case effectively becomes
the body initiating censorship of the disputed material.

## 4. Digital Censorship: From FIR to Takedown

The repression no longer stops with arrest. Andhra Pradesh has
developed a parallel censorship chain:

Political criticism → partisan complaint → police FIR →
platform request → removal or restriction.

Police stations are increasingly monitoring videos, identifying account
holders and communicating with global platforms. A local Circle Inspector
can send a request affecting content viewed by lakhs of citizens.

The disputed content may be restricted before any court determines
whether it is unlawful. An FIR, which is only an allegation and the
beginning of an investigation, is treated as though it were a judicial
verdict.

The subjects targeted are politically revealing. They include Amaravati
land transactions, capital expenditure, farmer grievances, electricity tariffs,
fertilizer scarcity, DSC recruitment, government medical colleges, TTD
ghee tenders, the Tirumala Laddu controversy, the Indapur–Heritage
connection, liquor, sand mining, crimes against women, custodial deaths
and corruption.

These are issues of public policy and public money. They should be
answered with records, inquiries and political debate. Instead, the content
is reported, criminalised and removed.

Opposition-linked pages such as Jagananna Connects, YSJ 2.0,
V-YSRCP, YSRCP Talks, Facebook pages, X handles, YouTube channels
and WhatsApp administrators have entered the enforcement net.

The updated register itself includes the YSRCP Official Page, official
WhatsApp administrators, Instagram in-charges, YSRCP Buzz, the
YSRCP Youth Wing and several identifiable pages and accounts. This
establishes that the target is no longer only the individual speaker. It is the
infrastructure through which opposition communication reaches the public.

text:
The takedown of YSRCP’s official Instagram handle and the
inaccessibility of its official Facebook page in India represent institutional
censorship of the principal opposition. These are not private accounts of
one activist. They are recognised political channels through which the
party communicates policies, evidence, press statements and public
grievances.

Restricting these platforms interferes with both the party’s right to speak
and the public’s right to receive political information.

The censorship has also become secondary. Journalists and
commentators who defended Prof. Nageshwar’s right to express an
opinion or questioned the criminal cases found their own content targeted.
The government is therefore not only punishing the original critic. It is
punishing those who challenge the punishment.

The real success of digital censorship cannot be measured only through
deleted posts. It lies in the content never published. Journalists avoid
investigations. Farmers refuse to record videos. Administrators decline to
share citizen grievances. Comedians remove political jokes. Television
producers avoid critical guests. Citizens leave WhatsApp groups.

The objective is anticipatory obedience: people should silence themselves
before the police or platform is required to act.

## 5. Selective Policing and Institutional Double Standards

The political character of the crackdown is exposed by the contrast
between the speed used against critics and the delay shown when
citizens seek protection from serious crime.

Police trace social media users across districts and States, but families of
missing children wait for answers. Teams are formed over political videos,
while complaints concerning crimes against women face delay. Critics are
arrested under non-bailable sections, while politically connected offenders
remain beyond immediate action.

The disappearance of little Gnaneshwari from Tuni, the reluctance to
register the sexual-assault complaint involving a mentally challenged girl
in Peddapuram, and the delayed action after a tribal woman was stripped
and assaulted in Kavali demonstrate this inversion of priorities.

text:
The Sai Krishna custodial-death controversy further damaged public
confidence. Serious questions were raised about custody, official
responsibility and the disappearance of his body. Instead of answering
those questions transparently, the government moved towards stronger
control of the social media through which the incident became public.

Other custodial deaths and suicides connected with police harassment
deepened the crisis. Yet the administration’s energy remained focused on
prosecuting those discussing police misconduct online.

The principle appears to be:

The police are not required to answer the questions. They are
empowered to act against the people asking them.

The same double standard applies online. Ruling-party ecosystems
circulate morphed images, personal attacks, degrading content against
women and character assassination without facing comparable action.

There are no equal waves of FIRs, midnight arrests, interstate teams or
organised-crime charges against government-aligned accounts. The
government’s claim that it is cleaning up social media therefore collapses.

A neutral policy would apply one standard to TDP, Jana Sena, YSRCP
and unaffiliated citizens. The present system protects abuse when it
serves power and criminalises criticism when it challenges power.

## 6. Courts Versus the Crackdown

As police safeguards weakened, courts became the last line of protection.

Families filed habeas corpus petitions simply to locate activists taken in
plain clothes. Courts examined contradictory arrest timings, demanded
CCTV and communication records, questioned serious sections and
refused mechanical remand.

In Savindra Reddy’s case, judicial scrutiny exposed inconsistencies
between the police account and independent evidence. In Sai Bhargav’s
case, the judge recorded his custodial-assault statement in camera,
ordered a medical examination and questioned the organised-crime
provision. In Khaja’s case, the magistrate held that notice procedure
should have been followed and ordered his release.

text:
These cases demonstrate that arrest does not automatically justify
remand. Courts must independently examine whether custody is
necessary, whether notice was issued, whether the section is applicable
and whether the accused poses a genuine risk.

For many social-media cases, the accused has a fixed residence and the
evidence already exists electronically. There is no legitimate need for
sudden arrest when notice under Section 35(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita can secure cooperation.

The government chooses arrest because notice does not produce the
same political spectacle.

Judicial resistance has limited individual abuse, but it cannot fully restore
what was lost. A person may be released after being paraded before the
media. A section may be rejected after reputation has been destroyed.
Bail may be granted after employment and income have been interrupted.

Police allegations receive immediate publicity. Judicial correction arrives
later and receives less attention.

This is why bail alone is insufficient. Officers who conceal custody, alter
timelines, coerce signatures, invoke manifestly inapplicable provisions or
mislead courts must face departmental and legal accountability. Without
consequences, the same method will be repeated against the next critic.

## 7. The Human Cost of Manufactured Fear

The case register records FIRs. It does not record the invisible sentence
imposed on families.

Activists spend their savings on lawyers, bail and travel. Daily-wage
workers lose income. Farmers leave agricultural work. Small businesses
close. Employees lose jobs or face disciplinary action. Phones essential
for work remain seized.

Young people face interrupted education, background-verification
problems and damaged employment prospects. A pending
organised-crime, narcotics or sexual-offence case can affect an entire
career before trial begins.

The stigma survives even when the case weakens. A person labelled a
drug offender or sexual offender remains searchable online. Children face
questions at school. Families endure public humiliation. Employers
hesitate. The arrest headline remains visible while the bail order is

Spouses and parents carry the burden of tracing detainees, arranging

exposed when both parents were drawn into police action. Savindra’s wife
had to approach the High Court to locate him. Tarak’s elderly parents
moved between stations seeking information.

Custodial violence also destroys trust in policing. Puli Sagar’s caste

The widest damage is the chilling effect. It is visible in the journalist who
drops a story, the student who closes an account, the farmer who refuses
to speak on camera, the comedian who removes a joke and the
government employee who declines to expose corruption.

These people will never enter the case register. Yet their silence is the
intended outcome of Emergency 2.0.

## Conclusion: From Political Vendetta to a Digital Police State

Andhra Pradesh’s Digital Emergency began with cases against YSRCP
social media activists. It expanded to women, students, journalists,
political analysts, YouTubers, comedians, page administrators, opposition
spokespersons and ordinary citizens.

- The progression is unmistakable.
- First came notices and station summons.
- Then came multiple FIRs for identical content.
- Midnight arrests and plainclothes pickups followed.
- Families were denied information.
- Phones were seized and networks mapped.
- Signatures were obtained in custody.
- Political communication was described as organised crime.
- When courts questioned those cases, narcotics, sexual-offence,
- extortion and extraordinary provisions were introduced.
